concept: Atlas Performance Advisor drop-index recommendations (unused, redundant, hidden)

claims.text: Atlas flags an index as unused when it has supported no query for at least seven days after creation or server restart; it inspects only the 20 most active collections for unused indexes. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-30)

Atlas always recommends dropping hidden indexes, but tells users to drop only after deciding they are unnecessary. Its hidden-index display covers the top 20 most active namespaces when the page loads, so it may omit others. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-30)

Review usage over a representative application cycle before removing an apparently unused index. Percona warns specifically about monthly reporting indexes; OneUptime likewise qualifies zero-access candidates by a representative observation period. (medium confidence)

Hide a candidate before dropping it to test query-planning impact; if performance regresses, unhide it. A hidden index remains maintained and is immediately available when unhidden, avoiding a rebuild. (medium confidence)

Server restarts reset index-usage counters, and changing an index between hidden and visible also resets its $indexStats. Account for these observation-window resets when reviewing removal evidence. (medium confidence)

Hiding does not remove index maintenance or storage costs: hidden indexes are updated on writes and continue consuming disk space and memory. A hidden trial therefore tests query dependence rather than the resource savings from actual removal. (medium confidence)
Atlas Performance Advisor recommends removing unused, redundant, and hidden indexes to reduce write overhead and recover storage. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-30)

Atlas labels a same-collection prefix index redundant: with {a:1,b:-1}, {a:1} is a candidate but {b:-1} is not. The related covering indexes shown beneath a candidate are not themselves removal recommendations. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-30)
Hiding a candidate removes it from query planning but retains write maintenance and storage costs. Unhiding restores availability without rebuilding the index. (medium confidence)
Before dropping based on usage counters, inspect every read-serving replica-set member: reads on another member can make one node appear to have an unused index. (medium confidence)

A zero access counter does not prove an index has no purpose: uniqueness checks and TTL expiration do not increment these read-usage counters. Hidden unique and TTL indexes still enforce uniqueness and expire documents, so a successful hide trial does not prove that losing those behaviors is safe. (medium confidence)

Prefix coverage alone is insufficient grounds for automatic removal: MongoDB's compound-index removal guidance assumes neither index has a sparse or unique constraint, qualifications omitted from OneUptime's simple redundancy example. (medium confidence)

Atlas's Drop Index dialog supplies shell commands for dropping or hiding and a link to the index-management UI; the user then executes the selected action through the UI or shell. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-30)

A June 2017 incident report for MongoDB 3.2.11 describes query latency increasing after dropping zero-use indexes. SERVER-29419 was closed as a duplicate of WT-3207, a checkpoint-wait issue; it is historical evidence, not proof of a current Atlas recommendation defect. (low confidence)

A practical validation sequence is to inspect usage and index definitions, hide the candidate, monitor representative queries for regressions, then drop only after validation; unhide if query performance regresses. (medium confidence)
